extracted.intended_audience: members of the House of Lords, policymakers, journalists, and the informed public
extracted.subtask_short: Hutton report debate on media conduct
extracted.subtask_description: House of Lords debate analysing the Hutton Inquiry, government handling of intelligence/dossiers, BBC journalism standards, and the relationship between government and the media. The text highlights criteria for responsible investigation, editorial practice, and government accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue the whole truth; avoid scapegoating
rubrics_metrics.description: "Finding scapegoats is the soft option. What matters is a determined search for the whole truth and a determination to learn for the future."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should focus on reconstructing complex responsibilities rather than assigning blame to individuals; aim to learn lessons and secure future peace/stability rather than merely punishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'sexing up' official documents or dossiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Dossier wording must not be embellished to make a case stronger than the intelligence warrants; 'sexing up' may mean exaggerating or over-egging interpretation or otherwise distorting impact by emphasis, omission or presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not convert cautious or qualified intelligence into stronger assertions for rhetorical or political effect (examples cited: changing wording from 'could' to 'are', boosting the prominence of the '45 minutes' claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require corroboration; do not rely on a single uncorroborated source
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of serious threats or operational capabilities should not be based on a single, uncorroborated source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek collateral evidence (satellite or air photographs, signals traffic, multiple intelligence streams). The transcript notes the 45-minute claim rested on one source and lacked supporting photographic/signals evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve qualifiers; avoid converting qualified language into definitive assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain careful wording (e.g. 'we judge' versus 'intelligence suggests'); changing qualified formulations to unqualified forms misleads readers about certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and authors should retain appropriate caveats and avoid overstating conclusions when the underlying intelligence is uncertain or tentative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal critical review: explicitly ask 'Are you sure?' before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafts and appendices lacked notes asking 'Are you sure?' or 'Have we got this right?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should build explicit critical checkpoints into drafting processes so contributors are prompted to re-check, corroborate, and question key assertions before release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to basic tenets of good journalism: check facts and correct promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hutton report was characterised as 'a story that was wrong' and criticised BBC management for not checking it even weeks after broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and news organisations must verify facts before and after publication, correct mistakes promptly, and, where appropriate, apologise publicly (the text stresses the importance and difficulty of apologising: 'I apologise').

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance transparency/public access with respect for legal/judicial process
rubrics_metrics.description: The public had greater access to this inquiry than any other in history, but the debate stresses that public opinion or polls should not substitute for judicial or authoritative findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure inquiries are sufficiently transparent for public trust while respecting the integrity of legal procedures and not letting media reaction override formal conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media must balance power with responsibility; do not substitute media for parliamentary accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning against the press arrogating to itself a role replacing Parliament ('a kind of House of Columns to replace a House of Commons').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism carries influence but must exercise corresponding responsibility and not seek to supplant democratic institutions or their accountability functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undue political pressure on editorial organisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Government communications (e.g. 'a blizzard of hectoring e-mails from Mr Alastair Campbell') can be inappropriate means of influencing editorial content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain editorial independence by insulating newsrooms from persistent political lobbying; correspondence from government should not dictate editorial conclusions or phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle witnesses and anonymity appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over Dr Kelly: whether anonymity was appropriate and whether he went beyond his remit in speaking to media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliaments, committees and media should exercise care when encouraging or granting anonymity, and be cautious in how witnesses are questioned or presented to avoid unfair pressure or misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define technical/legal terms clearly in public documents
rubrics_metrics.description: There was confusion about the meaning of 'weapons of mass destruction'—no universally acceptable definition was cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy documents and public statements should define key terms precisely so readers and decision-makers understand the scope and implications of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate, structured processes for important documents; avoid frenetic ad-hoc drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: The exchange of frantic e-mails and repeated drafts between officials shortly before publication was described as 'an inappropriate way of dealing with a matter of such immense importance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-stakes reports and dossiers should follow disciplined drafting, review and sign-off procedures rather than last-minute, emotionally driven editing by multiple actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require concrete operational evidence for claims of military readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that a force could deploy weapons in '45 minutes' should be supported by operational indicators (numbers of men, paperwork, signalling, communications changes, satellite imagery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should cite observable indicators (increased radio traffic, movement visible in air photos, logistical preparations) when making claims about force posture or readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institute editorial/governance reviews after failures of process
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls for reviews of BBC governors and the director-general in light of management failings over the disputed story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When significant editorial failures occur, organisations should conduct governance and editorial-process reviews to identify root causes and implement reforms.
